title: Trophies for All? Children's and Adolescents’ Reasoning About Inclusive Versus Selective Awards
abstract: ABSTRACT How do children and adolescents reason about the consequences of institutional reward systems? We examined developmental differences in reasoning about inclusive versus selective awards in a youth sports context. Participants in two age groups (43 in the 7‐ to 9‐year‐old age group and 44 in the 15‐ to 18‐year‐old age group; 46% female, 49% male, 5% other or preferred not to say; majority Asian/White; USA, 2024–2025) read scenarios in which trophies were awarded either to all participants or only to top performers in a running race and predicted motivational, emotional, and behavioral outcomes. Across age groups, participants expected selective awards to increase effort and pride, suggesting that by 7 years of age children recognize links between incentive structures and task engagement. By adolescence, systematic reasoning expanded to include the possibility that selective incentives could motivate behavior that conflicts with social norms or personal safety, including cheating and risk‐taking. In addition, adolescents’, but not children's, preferences for reward systems were systematically related to their own perceived running ability, suggesting that evaluations of incentive systems increasingly align with self‐interest across development. Together, these findings reveal both continuity and change in how young people reason about incentive systems: children as young as 7 linked reward systems to effort and pride, whereas adolescents additionally made inferences about self‐interest and norm‐conflicting behavior.
reasoning_research: The study uses a clear cross-sectional design with two age groups and hypothetical scenarios to assess developmental differences in reasoning about inclusive versus selective awards. However, the sample is relatively small, recruitment details are limited, and no preregistration or modeling is mentioned, limiting methodological rigor.
reasoning_impact: The findings are relevant to understanding how children and adolescents reason about incentive systems, effort, and norm-conflicting behavior such as cheating. This could inform educational and youth sports policies, and offers a developmental perspective on social norms and self-interest, though implications remain exploratory.

title: Nilai Emotional Spiritual Quotient (ESQ) dalam Novel Kami (Bukan) Sarjana Kertas Karya J.S Khairen Perspektif Psikologi Sastra
abstract: This study aims to identify and describe the Emotional Spiritual Quotient (ESQ) values represented in the novel Kami (Bukan) Sarjana Kertas by J.S. Khairen. Using a literary psychology perspective, the research explores the psychological development of the characters in responding to quarter-life crisis and spiritual challenges. This study employed a descriptive qualitative approach with library research as the primary method. Data consisted of narrative passages and dialogues collected through close reading and note-taking techniques and were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles and Huberman. The findings identified 30 data classified into seven ESQ indicators: honesty, responsibility, discipline, visionary, fairness, caring, and cooperation. Among these, caring emerged as the most dominant indicator, whereas no data representing fairness were identified. The findings reveal that the characters' emotional maturity and spiritual awareness develop through the interaction between internal psychological potential and environmental pressures. This study contributes to literary psychology by demonstrating that integrating the Emotional Spiritual Quotient (ESQ) provides a comprehensive framework for understanding character development and psychological resilience in contemporary Indonesian novels. The findings also highlight the relevance of ESQ values in interpreting existential challenges experienced by university students.
reasoning_research: The study uses a descriptive qualitative approach with library research, which is common in literary psychology but lacks the rigor expected in empirical decision neuroscience. No hypotheses, controls, or statistical analyses are provided; interpretation is subjective. The method is appropriate for literary analysis but offers little generalizable evidence.
reasoning_impact: The article focuses on ESQ values in an Indonesian novel and has negligible relevance to self-control, attention, or computational decision-making research. Its implications are confined to literary psychology and do not suggest new directions for experimental or theoretical work in the field.

title: Neurodevelopmental reward dysregulation and addiction risk in ADHD
abstract: Abstract Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with an elevated risk of substance use disorders (SUDs), yet most affected individuals do not develop addiction, indicating that vulnerability is selectively distributed rather than intrinsic to the disorder itself. This Review synthesizes current evidence on the neurodevelopmental mechanisms linking ADHD to SUD vulnerability, examines reward-related dysregulation as a unifying mechanistic framework underlying this association, and proposes a subgroup-based precision psychiatry perspective to explain the heterogeneity of addiction risk among individuals with ADHD. Integrating evidence across genetics, molecular neuroscience, neurodevelopment, systems-level circuitry, computational modeling, and environmental modulation, converging findings implicate polygenic variation affecting synaptic and dopaminergic pathways that interacts with atypical maturation of frontostriatal and frontocortical systems supporting reward valuation, inhibitory control, and salience processing. These multilayered perturbations may manifest computationally as dysregulated reinforcement learning, including altered dopamine signaling dynamics and impaired integration of delayed outcomes, biasing decision-making toward immediate reward. At the circuit level, disrupted coordination between mesolimbic reward systems and prefrontal control networks may facilitate a shift from goal-directed behavior to habit-based responding following repeated substance exposure, further shaped by experience-dependent neuroplasticity. Importantly, available evidence suggests that addiction risk is concentrated within distinct ADHD subgroups characterized by reduced responsiveness to anticipated rewards, impaired reinforcement learning, preference for immediate over delayed rewards, impaired inhibitory control, emotional dysregulation, and impulsive decision-making that emerge and evolve across development. Collectively, this synthesis supports a precision psychiatry framework integrating genetic, neuroimaging, computational, and digital phenotyping approaches to improve the identification, prediction, and prevention of SUD vulnerability in ADHD.
journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience

title: Behavioral finance as a factor in investment decision-making: the impact of cognitive biases on financial choices
abstract: The article examines the impact of cognitive biases on investment decision-making. It substantiates the need to analyze them not only as distinct manifestations of behavioral irrationality but also as interconnected mechanisms in financial decision-making. The theoretical framework of the study is based on bounded rationality and prospect theory. Five cognitive biases that significantly affect investment behavior are systematized as follows: loss aversion, overconfidence, confirmation bias, herding behavior, and anchoring. Based on a synthesis of theoretical propositions and empirical findings, a classification of cognitive biases according to their dominant mechanism of influence is proposed. Three groups are distinguished: belief-formation and belief-protection biases, reference-point-dependent biases, and social-inference biases. The cumulative nature of interactions among cognitive biases is substantiated. In particular, a sequential mechanism is identified in which overconfidence contributes to the formation of a persistent investment belief, confirmation bias reinforces it through selective information processing, and loss aversion increases the psychological cost of abandoning the initial decision. The relationship between anchoring and herding behavior is also examined, highlighting the need to distinguish social imitation from synchronized investor responses to common reference points. Differentiated approaches to mitigating the negative effects of cognitive biases are proposed for individual investors, financial advisers, and institutions. The findings demonstrate that corrective measures should target not only individual biases but also the underlying mechanisms and stages through which investment decisions are formed. Keywords: behavioral finance, investment decision-making, cognitive biases, loss aversion, disposition effect, overconfidence, confirmation bias, herding behavior, anchoring, investment behavior.
reasoning_research: The article is a theoretical synthesis based on bounded rationality and prospect theory, proposing a classification of cognitive biases in investment decision-making. It does not report original empirical data or preregistered methods, limiting methodological rigor. The conceptual organization of biases into three groups and the sequential mechanism is thoughtful but not novel enough for a high quality rating.
reasoning_impact: The framework may help structure future research on interactions among cognitive biases in financial decisions, particularly the sequential process and the distinction between herding and synchronized responses. However, without testable predictions or empirical validation, its direct influence on decision neuroscience or computational modeling is likely modest.
journal: Ukrainian Journal of Applied Economics and Technology

title: Decoding the Consumers of Hawker Food
abstract: Singapore’s Hawker Culture has gained increasing attention in the last few years, not just due to its inscription on UNESCO’s Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, but also due to growing concern about its preservation. A central dilemma Singapore faces is that although hawker food is acclaimed both domestically and internationally as a unique part of Singaporean cultural heritage, its practice is declining. Pre-existing studies focus on supply-side cost drivers or purely qualitative cultural narratives. In contrast, this study aims to apply quantitative methods to the lived experiences of current consumers of hawker food to better understand underlying demographic differences and their potential significance in the effort to preserve this piece of intangible cultural heritage. An online survey was conducted among Singaporean respondents, collecting data on demographics, taste preferences, and price-sensitivity scenarios to examine relationships among age, income, and price sensitivity. The findings reveal a U-shaped relationship between age and price sensitivity, driven by factors including affordability, access to home-cooked substitutes, social value, health considerations, and cultural value. Income exhibits a negative relationship with price elasticity of demand; however, even high-income consumers remain price elastic. The study also considers behavioral factors, including loss aversion, that influence consumer decision-making. These findings suggest that demographic characteristics can be used to tailor targeted preservation strategies and could provide a foundation for more consumer-centric quantitative research to sustain hawker culture.
reasoning_research: The study applies a survey-based quantitative approach to a novel cultural consumption context, examining demographic and price-sensitivity relationships. However, methodological details such as sampling strategy, survey validation, and statistical modeling are not described, limiting assessment of rigor.
reasoning_impact: The focus is on hawker food preservation, which is specific and not central to self-control or decision neuroscience. The findings may inform targeted policies for cultural heritage but have limited general theoretical impact.

title: Academic Integrity in Unsupervised Digital Environments: The Role of Interdisciplinary Task Design and Peer Assessment
abstract: ABSTRACT Academic cheating remains a persistent challenge in education across all levels despite various proposed solutions. This study is the first to investigate the integration of an interdisciplinary assessment approach and peer assessment as proactive strategies to enhance academic integrity in unsupervised digital learning environments. A quasi‐experimental study with control and experimental groups was conducted with N = 110 students enrolled in primary teacher education, including a control group ( n = 55) and an experimental group ( n = 55) over one semester. Academic integrity and cheating‐related behaviours were measured across three dimensions. The findings revealed statistically significant differences between the experimental and control groups across all dimensions (all p   0.14). In addition, Cohen's d values for all dimensions were ≥ 0.80, indicating substantial educational and practical significance. These findings suggest that the intervention was effective in reducing cheating behaviours and strengthening academic integrity in unsupervised digital learning environments. The study highlights the potential of integrating interdisciplinary assessment and peer assessment into contemporary teaching and assessment practices to promote more responsible learning behaviours.

title: Beyond the unitary self: Behavioral and drift–diffusion modeling evidence for a true self-prioritization effect and intra-self competition
Trans-SAC: gamification design for sustained user engagement in residential demand response
abstract: Abstract Residential Demand Response (DR) is a critical mechanism for maintaining the supply-demand balance in modern smart grids. While gamification has recently emerged as a promising strategy to incentivize residential participation, existing programs suffer from severe long-term user fatigue. Once the initial "novelty effect" wears off, users rapidly habituate to static rewards, leading to a precipitous decline in DR reliability. Furthermore, traditional pricing models and standard Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agents optimize purely for physical grid states, failing to capture the latent psychological dynamics of human participants.To address this critical gap, this paper proposes Trans-SAC, a novel gamification-aware dynamic DR framework that integrates psychological fatigue modeling with advanced machine learning. First, we formulate a mathematical behavioral model to quantify the accumulation and decay of user fatigue. Second, a Transformer-based module is employed to process long-sequence historical interaction logs, utilizing multi-head self-attention to predict the real-time cognitive engagement probability of each user. Finally, this psychological state is incorporated into the state space of a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) agent. Guided by entropy-regularized exploration, the SAC agent autonomously executes "intermittent reinforcement" by dynamically adjusting task difficulties and reward multipliers.Extensive simulations, which combine real-world electricity-consumption traces from the Pecan Street dataset with a synthetically generated gamification-behavior environment, demonstrate the potential effectiveness of the proposed framework. Over a continuous 12-month simulated period, Trans-SAC was found to mitigate the modeled user-habituation process, maintaining a simulated Load Reduction Achievement Rate (LRAR) of 85.6% and a simulated User Retention Rate of 84.2%. Crucially, by strategically restraining rewards for intrinsically motivated users and deploying high-value interventions only when critical fatigue is detected, Trans-SAC achieved a Unit Incentive Cost of $0.061/kWh, representing a 21.8% economic improvement over standard DRL baselines under the simulated behavioral assumptions detailed in Section 4.1.The results suggest that coupling cognitive state assessment with DRL achieves a favorable trade-off between long-term grid reliability and economic efficiency under the simulated behavioral assumptions of this study.
reasoning_research: The proposed Trans-SAC framework combines a mathematical fatigue model with a Transformer and Soft Actor-Critic agent, which is conceptually novel but validated only through simulations with a synthetic gamification-behavior environment. The reliance on explicitly stated simulated behavioral assumptions and the absence of human participant data limit methodological rigor regarding generalizability.
reasoning_impact: The work may influence gamification and deep reinforcement learning approaches in residential demand response, but its direct relevance to core self-control and attention research is modest. The findings are conditional on simulated assumptions and require empirical validation with real users to affect broader decision science theories.
journal: Journal of Engineering and Applied Science

title: Life is a Pressure Cooker: How and Why Stress Directs Consumers to Act Unethically
abstract: Abstract Unethical consumer behavior, such as deceptive product returns, digital piracy, shoplifting, and falsifying online reviews, is a growing concern with significant economic and ethical implications. However, its psychological antecedents remain underexplored. This research investigates the role of stress as a key driver of unethical consumer behavior, offering a novel perspective on why consumers engage in such conduct. Grounded in conservation of resources theory, we propose that stress heightens perceived threats to personal resources, triggering rumination—repetitive, negative thoughts about potential resource losses—which, in turn, fosters unethical behaviors. Across a field study and five experiments (one reported in the Online Appendix), we provide empirical evidence supporting this mechanism. Moreover, our findings reveal that the effect of stress on unethical consumer behavior is particularly pronounced among individuals with high levels of narcissism. These insights contribute to the broader understanding of consumer ethics and have important implications for marketers, human resource managers, and policymakers seeking to curb unethical consumer practices.
keywords: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment
Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification
reasoning_research: The study combines a field study and five experiments to test a clear, theory-driven mechanism linking stress to unethical consumer behavior via rumination. However, the abstract provides no details on sample sizes, preregistration, or robustness checks, limiting the ability to fully assess methodological rigor.
reasoning_impact: The research addresses an understudied antecedent of unethical consumer behavior and offers practical implications for marketers and policymakers. Its focus on stress and narcissism as moderators could inspire further work on individual differences in ethical decision-making, though the novelty is moderate given existing research on stress and unethical behavior.

title: Honesty in Causal Forests: When It Helps and When It Hurts
abstract: Causal forests estimate how treatment effects vary across individuals, guiding personalized interventions in areas like marketing, operations, and public policy. A standard practice is honest estimation—dividing the data into two samples, one to define subgroups and another to estimate treatment effects within them. This is intended to reduce overfitting and is the default in many software packages. But is it the right choice? We show that honest estimation can reduce the accuracy of estimates of individual treatment effects—especially when effect heterogeneity is substantial and datasets are large enough to detect it. The reason is a bias-variance trade-off: honesty lowers the risk of overfitting but increases the risk of underfitting by limiting the data available to detect and model heterogeneity. Across more than 7,000 benchmark datasets, we find that the cost of using honesty by default can be as high as requiring 27% more data to match the performance of models trained without it. Honesty is best understood as a form of regularization. Whether to adopt it should depend on the goals of the application and its empirical performance, not on reflexive default use.
reasoning_research: The study presents a conceptually novel challenge to a standard practice in causal forest estimation, backed by extensive benchmarking across over 7,000 datasets. Methodological rigor is strong for simulation-based research, though no human data are involved. The clear specification of bias-variance trade-offs and cost estimates adds robustness.
reasoning_impact: The findings are relevant primarily to the methodology of personalized intervention estimation, and do not directly address core themes of decision neuroscience or self-control. Potential influence is narrowly scoped within causal machine learning literature, limiting broader impact.
